e.etymology: A Spanish phonetic spelling of Byron, used across Latin America. Byron is an English surname from Old English byrum, at the cattle sheds.
A name with several sources: Thai mali, jasmine; a Welsh pet form of Mary, the counterpart of Molly; and a Norwegian short form of Magdalene or Amalie.

assoc.t: Mali, the West African country

e.etymology: A respelling of Josie, the pet form of Josephine, the feminine of Joseph, from Hebrew Yosef, he will add.
A modern name that joins lei, the Hawaiian flower garland, as in Leilani, to the -ana ending. It is also read as a spelling of Liana.
From Arabic salah, righteousness or goodness, often short for Salah al-Din, the name of the sultan known in the West as Saladin.

assoc.t: Mohamed Salah, Liverpool and Egypt soccer star
salah, the Islamic ritual prayer (a different word)

e.etymology: A modern American name, a spelling of Zaya in the sound family of Zara, Zaria and Maya. Zaya Wade, daughter of NBA star Dwyane Wade, put the name in the news in 2020.
An American respelling of Kailani, a Hawaiian name from kai, sea, and lani, sky or heaven.
A Spanish phonetic spelling of the English name Jamie, a pet form of James, common in Colombia. Its US peak followed Yeimy Montoya, heroine of the Colombian telenovela La Reina del Flow.
A respelling of Knox, a Scottish surname from a place name, from Old English cnocc, a round-topped hill.

assoc.t: Fort Knox, the US gold depository in Kentucky
Knox gelatine

e.etymology: A modern Indian name ending in ansh, from Sanskrit amsha, portion or part, in the pattern of Reyansh and Devansh.
A respelling of Denver, the Colorado city named for territorial governor James W. Denver. The surname comes from a village in Norfolk, England.

assoc.t: Denver, Colorado (sounds nearly the same)

e.etymology: A modern name that puts Day- in front of the -lani, sky or heaven, of Hawaiian names such as Leilani and Kailani.
A modern coinage from the Greek root xylo-, wood, familiar from xylophone, and a rhyme for Milo and Kylo.

assoc.t: xylophone, the instrument its sound recalls

e.etymology: From the surname Kirk, for someone who lived by a church, from the northern English and Scots word kirk, borrowed from Old Norse kirkja, church.
namesakes: Kirk Cameron (star of the sitcom Growing Pains)

assoc.t: Captain Kirk of Star Trek
Charlie Kirk, conservative activist killed in 2025

e.etymology: A name of mixed sources: a short form of Geneva, a link to Spanish nevar, to snow, and the Neva, the river of Saint Petersburg. It was most popular in the US around 1900.

assoc.t: Neva River in Saint Petersburg, Russia

e.etymology: A phonetic spelling of Giovanni, the Italian form of John, from Hebrew Yochanan, God is gracious. The J spellings are most common in Hispanic families.
A pet form of names beginning with Val-, such as Valeria and Valentine, from Latin valere, to be strong. It was given as a full name in the US around 1900.

assoc.t: sounds like valley

e.etymology: A spelling of Jayna or Jana, feminine forms in the John and Jane family. Fans know it from Jaina Solo of the Star Wars novels and Jaina Proudmoore of World of Warcraft.

assoc.t: Jaina Proudmoore of World of Warcraft
Jaina Solo, Han and Leia's daughter in Star Wars novels
Jaina, an adjective for the Jain religion

e.etymology: From Arabic salim, safe, sound or whole, from the root s-l-m that also gives salaam, peace, and Islam.

e.meaning: son of Fionnlagh, the fair warrior
e.etymology: A respelling of McKinley, a Scottish and Irish surname from Gaelic Mac Fhionnlaigh, son of Fionnlagh, a name meaning fair warrior.

assoc.t: William McKinley, 25th US president
Mount McKinley (Denali), highest US peak

e.etymology: From Arabic zaki, pure or virtuous, a word used in the Quran.
A name with several sources: Nara, the ancient capital of Japan; Korean nara, country; and a Brazilian girls' name. Its recent US rise tracks model and cooking creator Nara Smith.
namesakes: Nara Smith (model and TikTok cooking creator)

assoc.t: Nara, Japan, old capital famous for its deer

e.etymology: A modern American name in the sound family of Kamani, Armoni and Imani.
A modern blend of Scott or Scotland with the -lynn ending. Scott began as a surname for a Scot or a Gaelic speaker.

assoc.t: sounds like Scotland

e.etymology: An elaboration of Ezra, Hebrew for help, with an added -n. King Ezran is a young hero of the animated Netflix series The Dragon Prince, which began in 2018.

assoc.t: Ezran, boy king in Netflix's The Dragon Prince

e.etymology: A form of Marlene, the German blend of Maria and Magdalene made famous by Marlene Dietrich. Marlena Evans has been a lead character on the soap Days of Our Lives since 1976.
namesakes: Marlena Evans (Deidre Hall's character on Days of Our Lives)

e.etymology: The Spanish and Italian form of Gregory, via Latin Gregorius from Greek Gregorios, watchful or vigilant. Sixteen popes took the name.
A Scottish surname from a place in England, Old English hamel, blunt or flat-topped, and dun, hill. In the US it was given as a first name in honor of Alexander Hamilton.

assoc.t: Hamilton, the Broadway musical
Alexander Hamilton, Founding Father
Lewis Hamilton, Formula 1 champion
Hamilton watches

e.etymology: A respelling of Mallory, a Norman surname from Old French maloret, unlucky. It became a girls' name with Mallory Keaton of the 1980s sitcom Family Ties.
e.note: The root meaning, unlucky, puts some parents off.

e.etymology: A respelling of Tristan, the knight of the Tristan and Isolde legend. The name goes back to Celtic Drustan and was reshaped in French by triste, sad.
A respelling of Riley, an English surname from Old English ryge, rye, and leah, clearing, and also a form of the Irish surname Reilly.
From Hebrew Iyyov, related to a word for enemy and traditionally read as persecuted. Job is the man whose faith survives every loss in the Biblical Book of Job.
namesakes: Job (long-suffering hero of the Biblical Book of Job)

assoc.t: job, the everyday word for work (same spelling)

e.note: Spelled like the word job, so it is often misread; the name rhymes with robe.
